title: Decidability of discounted-sum universality over infinite words
formal: Is there an algorithm that, given a complete nondeterministic discounted-sum automaton \(\mathcal A\) with rational weights and a rational discount factor \(0<\lambda<1\), and a rational threshold \(t\), decides whether \(\mathcal A(w)\leq t\) for every infinite word \(w\in\Sigma^\omega\)? Here \(\mathcal A(w)\) is the infimum of the discounted sums of its runs on \(w\).
why: Universality asks whether a quantitative finite-state specification can keep every possible infinite input below a threshold. Its decidability is a basic unresolved boundary for verification with rational discounting, where arbitrarily small tail contributions can still decide exact threshold equality.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. importance.reason: A central decision problem for quantitative automata with direct connections to verification and exact discounted-sum representability; the rational infinite-word case goes beyond established restricted algorithms.

sentences: The input is a finite nondeterministic automaton whose transitions carry rational discounted costs.
Each infinite word receives the minimum cost among its runs, using one rational discount multiplier.
The problem asks whether every infinite word has value at most a supplied rational threshold.
The chosen run may depend on the entire word, and threshold equality must be decided exactly.
Known restricted discount factors and recent finite-word functional results do not supply the general algorithm requested here.

definitions: The input contains a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), finite nonempty state set \(Q\), initial state \(q_0\), finite transition set \(E\subseteq Q\times\Sigma\times Q\), and weight map \(g:E\to\mathbb Q\). Completeness means every state has at least one outgoing transition for each letter. There are no epsilon transitions, final-state restrictions or fairness conditions: every infinite run is eligible. On \(w=a_0a_1\cdots\), a run is an infinite state sequence \(q_0,q_1,\ldots\) with \(e_i=(q_i,a_i,q_{i+1})\in E\). Its value is \(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\lambda^i g(e_i)\); finite weights and \(0<\lambda<1\) ensure absolute convergence. The word value is \(\mathcal A(w)=\inf\{\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\lambda^i g(e_i): (e_i)_{i\geq0}\text{ is a run on }w\}\). The run set is nonempty and finitely branching, and this infimum is attained, so universality is equivalently \(\forall w\,\exists r\) with run value at most \(t\). Different words may use different runs; a run is not required to be chosen by an online strategy. One common discount factor applies to every transition. It is an input rational, not restricted to the reciprocal of an integer. All finite sets and tables are explicit; rational numerators and positive denominators are binary integers. An algorithm means one ordinary deterministic Turing machine that halts on every encoded valid instance and answers the exact non-strict threshold question. No finite-word truncation, approximation tolerance or bound on running time is imposed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating decision algorithm for the stated infinite-word, non-strict universality problem, including its correctness on every rational input. Alternatively prove in Lean that no such algorithm exists. A procedure for deterministic or functional automata, integer-reciprocal discount factors, finite words, strict inequalities alone or thresholds separated by a promised positive gap does not meet this full target without a proved reduction.

context_blocks.text: Discounting reduces the influence of distant transitions while retaining their exact contribution. For instance, an infinite run of weight one at every step has value \(1/(1-\lambda)\). A finite prefix determines an approximation, but equality to a rational threshold can depend on the entire continuation.

The 2014 source mentions universality as an unresolved problem related to exact-value discounted-sum games. This card fixes the standard non-strict infimum convention from the cited discounted-automata literature. The games problem is related but has different quantifiers and is not substituted for automaton universality.

Boker and Henzinger define universality by comparing every word value to a constant threshold. Their discount parameter is greater than one and divides the weight at each successive position; the present multiplier is its reciprocal. Their integral-parameter determinization result therefore covers integer-reciprocal multipliers, not all rational multipliers.

Nondeterminism is resolved separately for each complete word. Requiring one strategy to choose transitions from prefixes would impose an additional online restriction. Similarly, finding one favorable path in the underlying weighted graph would ignore the requirement to handle every input word.

The 2025 target-sum paper distinguishes strict from non-strict universality and finite from infinite words. Its universality and inclusion decidability theorem for functional automata appears in the finite-word part. Functional means that all accepting runs of each word have the same value; this is an additional restriction absent here.

For infinite words, the same paper develops connections to exact target discounted sums, including a hardness implication for strict universality and a result for instances where the corresponding generalized target sum has no solution. These are useful delineations of the remaining difficulty, rather than a decision theorem for every instance in this card.
